about: Espresso's blackcurrant-smelling odorant
text: One of espresso's key odorants is a compound with a long name, 3-mercapto-3-methylbutyl formate, which a 2021 review of espresso aroma lists with a blackcurrant-like smell.

about: Diones behind buttery notes
text: When tasters call a coffee 'buttery', chemists look to diones: a 2021 review of espresso aroma lists 2,3-butanedione and 2,3-pentanedione with buttery odours, the second one also caramel-like.

about: Furaneol, marshmallow and caramel
text: Coffee holds more than 1,000 volatile compounds; in a 2025 study furaneol was among the most aroma-active of the 85 it picked out, and sniffed on its own it was described as marshmallow and caramel.

about: Guaiacol and brewing water at 96 °C
text: Guaiacol, listed with a phenolic, spicy smell in a 2021 review of espresso aroma, is one of the compounds the review says appear in espresso when the brewing water reaches 96 °C or more.

about: WCR lexicon's canned-blueberry reference
text: To teach 'blueberry', World Coffee Research's sensory lexicon uses a tin of blueberries in light syrup: tasters sniff a teaspoon of the syrup in a covered glass, then taste the blueberries themselves.

about: WCR's melted-sugar reference for caramelised
text: For its strongest flavour reference for 'caramelised', World Coffee Research's lexicon has panellists melt white sugar in a heavy pan until light amber, pour it onto wax paper and break up the cooled sheet.

about: Citric and malic acid references in the lexicon
text: Citric and malic acids each have an entry of their own in World Coffee Research's lexicon, and panellists learn them from weak solutions of the pure acid in water, starting at 0.025% citric acid and 0.5 g per litre of malic.

about: WCR's coconut references and whiskey lactone
text: World Coffee Research's lexicon gives two references for 'coconut': a drop of imitation coconut extract on a cotton ball, and whiskey lactone, a molecule whose name points to another drink entirely.

about: Ester references for pineapple and apple
text: Some references in World Coffee Research's lexicon are single molecules: 'pineapple' can be calibrated with ethyl butyrate and 'apple' with ethyl hexanoate, two esters supplied by the flavour-standards firm FlavorActiV.

about: WCR lexicon's Grape-Nuts reference for malt
text: The reference World Coffee Research's lexicon gives for 'malt' is a breakfast cereal: a spoonful of Grape-Nuts in a covered glass for the aroma, and a small cup of it for the flavour.

about: Why WCR's nutty reference gained walnuts
text: While World Coffee Research's lexicon was being built, its panel swapped the reference for 'nutty' from almonds with hazelnuts to almonds with walnuts, because that blend came closer to what the word meant.

about: WCR's microwaved-banana reference for overripe
text: To calibrate 'overripe', World Coffee Research's lexicon has panellists freeze an overripe banana, microwave it for a minute, mash it and serve a teaspoon in a covered glass.

about: WCR lexicon's peach-stone reference
text: To teach the aroma of 'peach', World Coffee Research's lexicon has tasters sniff a clean peach stone in a covered glass; for the flavour, they taste dry peach jelly powder.

about: WCR's pomegranate entry and root vegetables
text: World Coffee Research's lexicon notes that the aroma of 'pomegranate' can recall root vegetables such as beetroot and carrot, and it calibrates the word with pure pomegranate juice.

about: Vanilla and vanillin in the WCR lexicon
text: World Coffee Research's lexicon keeps 'vanilla' and 'vanillin' apart: one reference for vanilla is chopped vanilla pods, while vanillin, the pure compound, is linked with marshmallows and candyfloss.

about: WCR lexicon's Cabernet reference for winey
text: In World Coffee Research's lexicon, tasters learn 'winey' by sniffing half a cup of Cabernet Sauvignon in a large covered glass, a reference rated 10 on the lexicon's 15-point intensity scale.

about: Linalool: floral, lemon and rose in one molecule
text: One molecule can sit behind several tasting-note words: in a 2025 study of coffee aroma, sniffers described linalool on its own as floral, lemon and rose.

about: Pyrazines behind nutty and cocoa notes
text: In a 2025 study that sniffed coffee's aroma compounds one by one as they left a gas chromatograph, individual pyrazines were described as nuts, peanuts, almond, popcorn, and coffee and cocoa.

about: Roasting raises vanillin in arabica
text: Vanillin is already present in raw arabica beans, and a 2000 study found that roasting raised it strongly, along with other potent odorants such as β-damascenone and 4-vinylguaiacol.

about: 4-Vinylguaiacol and smoky notes
text: In a 2025 study of commercial coffees, 4-vinylguaiacol was among the most influential aroma compounds, with an odour activity value of 761 in one sample; sniffed on its own, it was described as smoky.

about: Black tea in the flavour wheel's floral family
text: On the 2016 SCA and World Coffee Research flavour wheel, 'black tea' sits in the floral family, beside chamomile, rose and jasmine. The families grew out of 72 experts sorting the words online, without tasting.

about: Why the flavour wheel's colours matter
text: The colours on the SCA flavour wheel were picked to evoke each word, so a taster stuck at 'some kind of red fruit' can run an eye over the wheel's red-coloured words to find a closer match.

about: The coffee belt between the tropics
text: Most coffee grows in a narrow band around the Equator, between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, where the plant finds the rich soil, mild temperatures, seasonal rain and dappled shade it likes.

about: Bee variety and arabica fruit set
text: Arabica can pollinate itself, yet bees still matter. Across 24 agroforestry plots in Indonesia, fruit set rose from about 60% where three bee species visited the flowers to about 90% where twenty did.

about: The berry borer's eggs, seen by micro-CT
text: The coffee berry borer spends most of its life hidden inside the cherry, so researchers used micro-CT scans to watch it. Its eggs are laid in order, starting at the edge of the seed and working inwards.

about: The coffee berry borer's gut bacteria
text: The coffee berry borer, coffee's most damaging insect pest, can cut a crop by up to 80%. It copes with caffeine thanks to gut bacteria, including Pseudomonas, that break it down and even live on it.

about: Coffee's caffeine evolved on its own
text: Coffee most likely did not get its caffeine from an ancestor it shares with tea or cacao. Reading the robusta genome in 2014 showed its caffeine-making genes are closer kin to other coffee genes than to theirs.

about: Caffeine in coffee nectar and bee memory
text: Coffee flowers carry a little caffeine in their nectar. In a 2013 study, honeybees given caffeine with their reward were three times as likely to remember a flower's scent as bees fed sugar alone.

about: Leaf rust ends Ceylon's coffee
text: In 1870 Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, exported some 53,000 tonnes of coffee. Then leaf rust took hold: by 1890, 90% of its coffee land had been abandoned, and the island turned to tea instead.

about: The layers of a coffee cherry
text: Peel a coffee cherry and you pass a thin skin, then the pulp, then the parchment, a thin layer that guards each bean, and finally the silverskin, a tissue that supported the bean as it first grew.

about: The derriçadeira hand-held shaker
text: Between hand and machine sits the derriçadeira: a long pole tipped with two vibrating 'hands'. Pickers spread a sheet under the tree, raise the pole into the branches, and the shaking brings the cherries down.

about: Harry Marshall Ward and leaf rust
text: Around 1880, Kew sent Harry Marshall Ward, a young Cambridge graduate, to Ceylon. In two years there he proved that a fungus caused coffee leaf rust and worked out its life cycle, but he had no way to stop it.

about: How coffee harvesting machines work
text: Coffee harvesting machines knock cherries loose with rotating, vibrating rods, then catch them and carry them to a bin. Tuning the vibration and arm speed lets them favour the ripest fruit, but they need fairly flat land.

about: Peaberries, the one-bean cherries
text: Most coffee cherries hold two beans, but in about 5% of the world's coffee the cherry carries just one, called a peaberry. Some are sorted out by hand to be sold on their own.

about: Leaf rust reaches the Americas
text: Coffee leaf rust turned up in Brazil in 1970. Within roughly twelve years, every major coffee country in the Americas had it.

about: How leaf rust spores spread
text: Leaf rust spores ride the wind and rain and hitch lifts on workers, birds and insects. They can survive for months, and on a coffee leaf in the right conditions can get inside within a few hours.

about: What coffee leaf rust looks like
text: Coffee leaf rust shows as pale-yellow spots on top of a leaf, with yellow-orange powdery spores beneath. It seldom kills the plant outright: the leaves drop, the beans are starved, and yields plunge.

about: Selective picking versus strip picking
text: Selective pickers work back through the same trees every eight to ten days, taking only the ripe cherries each time. Strip picking, by hand or machine, clears a whole branch in one go.

about: Shade coffee, forest and birds in Colombia
text: In Colombia's Eastern Andes, a study with Smithsonian bird scientists found dense, varied shade coffee helped many birds, from insect-eaters to nectar-feeders. Birds were also likelier to turn up where more forest stood within 2 km.

about: Smallholders grow most of the world's coffee
text: Coffee is mostly a small farmer's crop: some 25 million smallholders grow it, and farms under roughly 2 to 5 hectares are thought to make up 80% of coffee farms and grow about 60% of the world's coffee.

about: Three to four years to first fruit
text: A newly planted coffee tree takes about three to four years to bear its first fruit, depending on the variety. When ripe, the cherries of most varieties turn a deep red to purple.

about: Tall trees with flowers and fruit at once
text: Left unpruned, a coffee tree can grow taller than 9 m. One plant can carry flowers, bright green cherries and ripe purplish ones all at the same time.

about: Climate projections for wild arabica
text: A 2012 Kew-led study modelled wild arabica in its native forests and projected that, by 2080, the area with a suitable climate could shrink by 38% at best and by about 90% at worst.

about: Wild coffee species at risk
text: When Kew scientists assessed all 124 wild coffee species in 2019, at least 60% were threatened with extinction, and 45% were not held in any genebank collection.

about: How much coffee one tree yields
text: An average coffee tree yields about 4.5 kg of cherries a year, which makes only around 1 kg of green coffee. Most trees give their best crops between about seven and twenty years old.

about: Bezzera's patent and Pavoni's Ideale
text: In the early 1900s Luigi Bezzera patented a brewing group that made each coffee fresh, to order. Desiderio Pavoni bought the patent, and the Ideale machine he built on it was first shown at Milan's 1906 Universal Exhibition.

about: Why the cappuccino is named after friars
text: The cappuccino is named after the Capuchin friars. Their own name comes from cappuccio, Italian for 'hood', and the drink took it from the brown of their hooded habits.

about: Cup of Excellence and its online auction
text: The Cup of Excellence began in Brazil in 1999. To sell that first year's winning coffees to the highest bidders, its team built coffee's first online auction.

about: De Clieu's seedling for Martinique
text: The story goes that in 1723 the young naval officer Gabriel de Clieu took a seedling from the French king's coffee tree and carried it to Martinique, through storms, a pirate attack and a saboteur. Within 50 years the island had over 18 million coffee trees.

about: How Decent Espresso began
text: Decent Espresso began when John Buckman, frustrated that his high-end home machines gave no live feedback and let temperatures swing, backed a computer-driven coffee machine on Kickstarter. When it collapsed, he stepped in and promised its stranded backers a working machine.

about: Java and the Mocha Java blend
text: The Dutch got coffee growing on Java in the late 1600s, and pairing it with Yemen's 'Mocha' gave Mocha Java, often called the world's first coffee blend.

about: The Faema E61 of 1961
text: The Faema E61 of 1961 swapped hand levers for an on/off switch and an electric pump holding a steady 9 bar, which became the standard for Italian espresso. Its boiler was turned on its side, keeping the machine low enough for the barista to talk to customers over it.

about: Gaggia's 1938 Lampo group
text: Achille Gaggia's 1938 patent was for 'Lampo', a group that pushed hot water through the coffee by pressure instead of steam. On the back of his machines he put the slogan 'Crema caffè naturale – funziona senza vapore': natural coffee crema, works without steam.

about: Gaggia's 1947 spring-lever machine
text: Achille Gaggia's lever design of 1947 had the barista pull a lever to load a spring, which then drove a piston through the coffee at 8 to 10 bar. A shot was 'pulled' in 25 to 30 seconds.

about: The legend of Kaldi and his goats
text: Legend has it that a goat herder named Kaldi saw his goats grow so lively after eating the cherries of a certain tree that they wouldn't sleep at night. In the story, a monastery's abbot made a drink from the cherries to stay awake through evening prayers.

about: La Marzocco GS, the first dual boiler
text: La Marzocco's GS of 1970 was the first machine with two separate boilers and saturated groups; GS stands for 'Gruppo Saturo'. One boiler could make steam without changing the temperature of the other, which held the brew water.

about: How La Marzocco got its lion name
text: La Marzocco was founded in Florence in 1927 by the brothers Giuseppe and Bruno Bambi. It is named after the Marzocco, the lion that stands for Florence, which sat on top of the brothers' new machine.

about: Moriondo's 1884 steam-and-water machine
text: Angelo Moriondo of Turin patented a coffee machine using both steam and water in 1884 and showed it at that year's General Italian Exhibition. None of his machines survive; the one in the MUMAC museum is a 2018 replica built from his patent.

about: Palheta and the bouquet of coffee seeds
text: As the story goes, coffee reached Brazil in a bouquet. Francisco de Mello Palheta, a Portuguese officer, was sent to French Guiana for seedlings; the French wouldn't share, but the governor's wife, taken with him, gave him flowers with coffee seeds hidden inside.

about: Qahveh khaneh, the 'Schools of the Wise'
text: By the 1500s, public coffeehouses called qahveh khaneh had sprung up in cities across the Middle East, with music, performances, chess and news alongside the coffee. They mattered so much for passing on news that they were also known as 'Schools of the Wise'.

about: SCAA and SCAE unite as the SCA in 2017
text: The Specialty Coffee Association was formed in 2017, when two older bodies joined: the Specialty Coffee Association of America, set up in 1982, and the Specialty Coffee Association of Europe, formed in 1998.

about: The first World Barista Championship, 2000
text: The first World Barista Championship, in Monte Carlo in 2000, had some 17 baristas making nine drinks for three judges. Mirrors were fitted above the espresso machines so spectators could see what the baristas were doing.

about: Fuego's eruptions and Acatenango's soil
text: Acatenango's farms lie beside Fuego, Spanish for 'fire', a volcano whose frequent eruptions keep topping up the coarse, sandy soil with minerals. Much of the coffee grows under thick shade, as high as about 2,000 m.

about: Mislabelled Antigua coffee and APCA's founding
text: In the early 2000s Antigua's growers reckoned the valley made at most 80,000 bags of green coffee, while 180,000 to 300,000 bags left Guatemala labelled Antigua. Their association, APCA, founded in 2000, set out to certify the real thing.

about: Antigua's three volcanoes and pumice soil
text: Antigua's valley is ringed by three volcanoes: Agua, Fuego and Acatenango. Its soil carries volcanic pumice, which holds water and helps the coffee cope with the valley's low rainfall.

about: The FNC's 1927 founding in Medellín
text: Colombia's coffee growers' federation, the FNC, was created in Medellín, Antioquia, in 1927, and Antioquia's own growers' committee began work at almost the same time.

about: Atitlán's Xocomil wind
text: Nine-tenths of Atitlán's coffee grows on the slopes of the three volcanoes that tower over Lake Atitlán. Every day a wind called the Xocomil churns the cold lake water and shapes the farms' microclimate.

about: Coffee as a ceremony gift in Kintamani, Bali
text: In Kintamani, on Bali, coffee is a customary gift at weddings, tooth-filing ceremonies and times of mourning, when neighbours and relatives bring it to be shared during the ceremony.

about: Kintamani, Indonesia's first GI product
text: In 2008 arabica from Kintamani, in the north of Bali, became the first Indonesian product recognised with a Geographical Indication certificate, after local farmers and processors applied for it together.

about: Boquete and Volcán either side of Volcán Barú
text: Panama's best-known coffee regions face each other across Volcán Barú, the country's tallest mountain: Boquete lies to its east and south-east, and the region called Volcán to its west and south-west.

about: Bolivia's Yungas and its smallholders
text: Bolivia's coffee grows mainly in the Yungas, mountains and valleys that fall from the high Altiplano around La Paz down towards the Amazon rainforest. Land reforms have returned land to smallholders, most of them indigenous, who grow most of its coffee.

about: Esmeralda's El Velo variety trial
text: In 2007 Boquete's Hacienda La Esmeralda began a decade-long variety trial, planting more than 400 different accessions high up at El Velo, in the hope of finding another coffee as remarkable as its Gesha.

about: Brazil, top coffee producer for 150 years
text: Brazil has been the world's biggest coffee producer for more than 150 years.

about: Ryo Mizuno's Café Paulista and Brazil's coffee
text: In 1908, the year the first Japanese emigrants arrived in Brazil, São Paulo state agreed to give Ryo Mizuno free coffee for three years if he opened coffee shops in Japan. His Café Paulista, founded in 1910, had its main shop in Ginza.

about: Brazil's National Coffee Day, 24 May
text: Brazil's National Coffee Day falls on 24 May. The date, set in 2005 by the coffee industry association ABIC, marks the start of the harvest in most of the country's growing regions.

about: Brazil's slow coffee start after 1727
text: Brazil was a slow starter: after coffee seedlings arrived from French Guiana in 1727, almost 80 years passed before it exported meaningful amounts. In 1800 its coffee exports were still close to nothing.

about: Cajamarca sweeps Peru's first Cup of Excellence
text: Peru's first Cup of Excellence, in 2017, was won by a coffee from Juan Heredia Sanchez in Cajamarca, scoring 92.25 points; the two next-highest scorers came from Cajamarca too.

about: Caranavi's clean sweep at Bolivia's 2004 CoE
text: All 13 winning lots at Bolivia's 2004 Cup of Excellence came from Caranavi, in La Paz department. First place went to a lot pooled from 82 farmers.

about: Caranavi, a 1960s pioneer settlement
text: Caranavi began in the early 1960s as a pioneer settlement, when a road was pushed down into Bolivia's lower Yungas. Most newcomers to the La Paz Yungas were Aymara-speaking farmers from the Altiplano, growing coffee, cacao and fruit.

about: Cauca's mountain shield from the Pacific
text: Cauca's coffee farms lie behind high Andean ranges that shield them from strong winds and damp air off the Pacific, one of the traits written into the region's denomination of origin in 2011.

about: Coffee's retreat from Costa Rica's Central Valley
text: Coffee from Costa Rica's Central Valley fell by almost two-thirds between the 1999–2000 and 2016–17 harvests, an ICAFE study found, from about 772,000 to 273,000 fanegas of cherry. Spreading towns, leaf rust and low prices all played a part.

about: Cerrado Mineiro, Brazil's first coffee GI
text: Cerrado Mineiro was the first Brazilian coffee region to win a geographical indication, in 2005, and became a denomination of origin in 2013. Its coffee grows at about 800 to 1,300 m.

about: Chanchamayo's 'coffee capital' mark
text: In 2022 the certification mark 'Chanchamayo, capital cafetalera del Perú' (Peru's coffee capital) was registered with Indecopi, as Chanchamayo worked towards a denomination of origin for its coffee.

about: Café Chiapas appellation of origin, 2003
text: In 2003 Mexico made 'Café Chiapas' a protected appellation of origin, reserved for Arabica grown in the state above 800 m, a band that held about three-quarters of its coffee land.

about: Cobán's chipi-chipi mist
text: Cobán, Guatemala's rainforest coffee region, has no real dry season, only wet and wetter months. A fine mist known as the chipi-chipi sinks from the clouds over its rolling hills, where the coffee grows in limestone and clay.

about: Bahareque in Colombia's Coffee Cultural Landscape
text: In 2011 UNESCO listed Colombia's Coffee Cultural Landscape as World Heritage. Its traditional buildings use bahareque: walls on a timber frame, covered with mats of guadua, a tough native bamboo.

about: Café de Colombia's EU protected status
text: In 2007 'Café de Colombia' became a Protected Geographical Indication in the European Union. The growers' federation had applied in 2005, the first such application for a product from outside the EU.

about: Juan Valdez and his mule Conchita
text: Juan Valdez, the fictional grower who travels with his mule Conchita, was introduced by Colombia's coffee federation in the late 1950s. Carlos Sánchez played him in print and on screen from 1969 to 2006.

about: Colombia's mitaca, the second harvest
text: Besides its main harvest, Colombia has a smaller second one, usually about six months later, which growers call the mitaca or traviesa.

about: The machines behind Costa Rica's micromills
text: Costa Rica's micromills grew out of compact, low-water demucilaging machines made by Penagos in Colombia and Pinhalense in Brazil. With them, farmers who used to sell their cherries to big mills could process their own coffee, and their neighbours'.

about: San José's National Theatre and its coffee tax
text: San José's National Theatre began with a coffee tax: in 1890 wealthy growers and merchants proposed five centavos on every arroba of coffee exported. It raised only about 133,000 pesos before an import duty replaced it; the theatre cost over three million.

about: Costa Rica's oxcarts on the coffee road
text: From the mid-1800s, oxcarts hauled Costa Rica's coffee from the Central Valley over the mountains to the Pacific port of Puntarenas, a trip of 10 to 15 days. Each cart was built to ring its own chime as its wheels turned.

about: Santo Domingo coffee and Dominican regions
text: Dominican coffee is sometimes sold as 'Santo Domingo', the country's old name. Most of it comes from smallholders who grow it in shade, and the country's coffee authorities recognise seven official regions, including Cibao and Barahona.

about: Ecuador's instant coffee exports in 2014
text: In 2014 about 87% of Ecuador's coffee exports left as soluble (instant) powder. The country's own crop was not enough to feed its soluble factories, which also brought in robusta from Vietnam.

about: El Salvador's 1970s rank as a coffee producer
text: In the early 1970s El Salvador was the world's fourth- or fifth-largest coffee producer by volume. Later it made its name instead with elite specialty coffees.

about: El Salvador's long loyalty to Bourbon
text: From the 1930s on, Salvadoran growers kept faith with the heirloom Bourbon. Before leaf rust struck in 2012–13, Bourbon trees, among them a widely grown selection called Tekisic, gave an estimated seven-tenths of the country's coffee.

about: El Salvador's 2012–13 leaf-rust losses
text: When leaf rust swept Central America in 2012–13, El Salvador was hit hard: its prized Bourbon and Pacamara trees resist the disease poorly, and the country's harvest fell by about 60% from one season to the next.

about: Espírito Santo's conilon since 1912
text: Espírito Santo's conilon story began in 1912, when Governor Jerônimo Monteiro introduced this Coffea canephora coffee to the state. It has since become Brazil's leading conilon grower, with about 70% of the country's crop in the years around 2020.

about: Ethiopia's first Cup of Excellence, 2020
text: Ethiopia held its first Cup of Excellence only in 2020. More than 1,400 lots were entered, and with travel halted by the pandemic, the international jury cupped the finalists in their own labs around the world.

about: Ethiopia's Yirgacheffe, Sidamo and Harar trademarks
text: In a scheme begun in 2004, Ethiopia registered Yirgacheffe, Sidamo and Harar as trademarks abroad, then licensed the names free of royalties to roasters and importers. By mid-2009 almost a hundred licence agreements had been signed.

about: Pacaya's ash on the Fraijanes plateau
text: Now and then Pacaya, one of Guatemala's active volcanoes, dusts the Fraijanes plateau with a fine layer of ash, topping up the pumice soil the coffee grows in with fresh minerals.

about: Hacienda El Progreso on San Cristóbal
text: On San Cristóbal in the Galápagos, Manuel J. Cobos turned Hacienda El Progreso into an industrial sugar plantation after 1879, and planted some 1,200 acres (about 490 hectares) with coffee, maize, fruit trees and other crops.

about: Gayo coffee around Lake Tawar
text: Aceh's Gayo coffee grows on the hills around Lake Tawar, a crater lake beside the town of Takengon. It is usually grown under managed shade, by smallholders who are often members of cooperatives.

about: Gayo coffee's Dutch beginnings, 1908
text: Coffee in Aceh's Gayo highlands goes back to 1908, when a Dutchman named Veenhuyzen first developed it there. For a decade it stayed a small, non-commercial crop, until the Wilhelmina Blang Gele plantation opened in 1918.

about: Gedeo Cultural Landscape, World Heritage site
text: In 2023 UNESCO made the Gedeo Cultural Landscape in Ethiopia a World Heritage site. On its slopes, tall trees shade enset, the local staple crop, and coffee grows in the layer beneath.

about: Guatemala's 2018 coffee heritage decree
text: In 2018 a ministerial decree named the traditional knowledge of growing coffee a symbol of Guatemalan identity, part of the nation's intangible heritage.

about: Guatemala's SHB altitude grade
text: On a Guatemalan sack, SHB stands for strictly hard bean: an altitude grade, not a cupping score, for coffee grown from about 1,370 m. Up there the cherries ripen slowly, so the beans grow harder and denser.

about: How coffee reached the Guianas and Brazil
text: Coffee came to the Guianas from the Indian Ocean, carried by Dutch and French trading companies, and from the Guianas it went on to Brazil.

about: Honduras's Lempira hybrid and new rust strains
text: Many Honduran farms were replanted with rust-resistant hybrids carrying Robusta genes, such as Lempira and IHCAFE 90. In 2017 Lempira fell to a new strain of leaf rust, one of as many as four new strains found in Honduran fields.

about: Honduras's six coffee regions
text: Honduras's coffee authorities have marked out six coffee regions. Three of them, Copán, Opalaca and Montecillos, line the mountain range along the borders with Guatemala and El Salvador, and tend to grow the country's highest coffees.

about: Huehuetenango's frost-guarding Tehuantepec winds
text: Huehuetenango is the highest and driest of Guatemala's three coffee regions without a volcano. Hot, dry winds from Mexico's Tehuantepec plain keep frost off its mountains, so coffee grows up to about 2,000 m.

about: Huila's altitude and cloud cover
text: Huila's coffee grows between about 1,000 and 2,200 m under frequent cloud: its denomination of origin, granted in 2013, cites only about 3.5 hours of sunshine a day.

about: Baba Budan's seven beans
text: Legend has it that Indian coffee began with seven beans: the saint Baba Budan is said to have brought them from Yemen and planted them in the Karnataka hills now named after him, the Baba Budangiris.

about: India's Kaapi Royale robusta
text: 'Kaapi Royale' names one of India's speciality robustas, not an estate: bold Robusta Parchment AB beans drawn from Coorg, Wayanad, Chikmagalur and Travancore.

about: India's Kents arabica and leaf rust
text: India's Kents coffee takes its name from the English planter who selected it early in the 20th century. Because it held up better against leaf rust, it stayed a favourite with Indian growers until the 1940s.

about: India's Mysore Nuggets Extra Bold
text: 'Mysore Nuggets Extra Bold' names neither a farm nor a single region: it is one of India's speciality coffees, made from very large, bluish-green washed arabica beans grown in several regions, among them Chikmagalur, Coorg and the Baba Budangiris.

about: India's two-tier shade canopy
text: Indian coffee grows beneath two layers of shade trees, including evergreen legumes, and nearly 50 kinds of shade tree have been found on its plantations. The trees also pull nutrients up from deep in the soil.

about: Jamaica Blue Mountain's early fame and its board
text: Jamaica Blue Mountain was already prized in the early 1800s, when the island was for a short while the world's leading coffee producer. After the Second World War a newly formed Coffee Industry Board took control of quality to guard the name.

about: Jamaica Blue Mountain's altitude rule and fog
text: To carry the Jamaica Blue Mountain name, coffee must grow between about 910 and 1,700 m; coffee from just below is sold as Jamaica High Mountain. Near-constant fog on the high slopes slows the coffee's growth, so its beans are denser than such heights usually give.

about: East Java's Ijen-Raung estates
text: Java's big traditional arabica estates, among them Kayumas, Pancur, Jampit and Blawan, lie in the Ijen-Raung highlands at the island's eastern end. The four largest are run by the government.

about: Kafa, birthplace of wild Arabica
text: UNESCO calls Kafa, in south-west Ethiopia, the birthplace of wild Arabica. A biosphere reserve since 2010, it is said to shelter nearly 5,000 wild varieties of the coffee plant.

about: Kona's coffee-picking school holiday
text: From 1932 until 1969, Kona's public schools took their long break from August to November instead of June to September, so that children could help pick the coffee harvest.

about: North and South Kona's soils
text: Kona has two halves: North Kona, on the slopes above Kailua-Kona, has mostly deep soil, while in South Kona the soil is younger and sometimes so thin that coffee trees grow straight out of holes and cracks in part-weathered lava.

about: Kona Nightingales, the coffee donkeys
text: Kona's coffee was once carried down its steep slopes by donkeys nicknamed 'Kona Nightingales'. In the late 1940s surplus military Jeeps took over the job.

about: Samuel Ruggles brings coffee to Kona, 1828
text: Kona's coffee goes back to 1828, when the Rev. Samuel Ruggles planted cuttings there from trees that Chief Boki, governor of Oʻahu, had brought back from Brazil three years earlier.

about: Laos, the Bolaven Plateau and robusta
text: Coffee reached Laos with French colonists in the early 1900s, and the Bolaven Plateau soon became its main growing area. Arabica came first, until leaf rust and hard weather pushed farmers to robusta; growers have since worked to revive arabica.

about: Lintong's plateau south-west of Lake Toba
text: Lintong coffee comes from one compact district, Lintongnihuta, just south-west of Lake Toba: a high, rolling plateau of clay soils under ferns, where smallholders grow it mostly without shade and largely without chemicals.

about: Machu Picchu–Huadquiña's slow-ripening microclimate
text: Café Machu Picchu–Huadquiña, a Peruvian denomination of origin, comes from a former hacienda in Santa Teresa, Cusco, near the snowy peaks of Salkantay, Sacsarayoc and Humantay, whose microclimate makes the cherries ripen slowly.

about: Manabí's coffee grown by the sea
text: In Las Piñas, near Manta on Ecuador's Pacific coast, coffee is grown just 40 to 250 m above sea level, close to the ocean, while elsewhere in Ecuador the average is about 1,200 m.

about: Mantiqueira de Minas and its small farms
text: When Mantiqueira de Minas, a group of 25 municipalities in southern Minas Gerais, won its denomination of origin in 2020, about four in five of its 8,200 growers farmed small coffee properties.

about: Marcala, Central America's first appellation
text: Marcala, in the highlands of western Honduras near the border with El Salvador, became Central America's first registered appellation of origin in 2005. It takes in some of the country's highest coffee-growing towns.

about: Mexico's indigenous smallholder coffee farmers
text: Almost all of Mexico's coffee is grown on small farms, and an estimated 85% of its coffee farmers are indigenous. In the south, many communities keep old traditions of communal self-government that lend themselves to co-operatives.

about: Myanmar's Shan State coffee goes specialty
text: Coffee from Myanmar's Shan State long crossed informally into China and Thailand, sold far below market rates. A five-year programme from 2014 linked its smallholders to world buyers, and in 2016 Myanmar's first commercially available specialty coffee was served in Washington.

about: Nariño, Colombia's first regional origin
text: In 2011 Colombia's industry regulator made Café de Nariño the country's first regional coffee denomination of origin, the result of a study of the region's coffee begun in 2006.

about: Hira Giri and Nepal's first coffee
text: The story goes that coffee reached Nepal in 1938, when a hermit named Hira Giri travelled to Aapchaur in Gulmi district with seeds from Burma. Farmers passed the plant along for more than four decades before commercial growing took off in the mid-1980s.

about: Nicaragua's half-dried coffee and better roads
text: Small Nicaraguan farms often sent half-dried coffee down from cloudy highlands to big mills in the sunnier lowlands to finish drying, and hold-ups on the way could ruin a lot. Better roads have since eased the trip.

about: Maracaturra, a Maragogipe and Caturra cross
text: Maracaturra, also called Maracatu, crosses the giant-beaned Maragogipe with the compact Caturra. Where it began is debated; one account credits the Nicaraguan farmer Byron Corrales and his father.

about: Where Nicaragua grows its coffee
text: Nicaragua grows almost all its coffee in the highlands of its north and centre, up towards the Honduran border: in Matagalpa and, further north, Jinotega and Nueva Segovia.

about: Norte de Santander's coffee-planting penance
text: The story goes that around 1834 Francisco Romero, a priest in Salazar de las Palmas in Norte de Santander, set his parishioners an unusual penance: planting coffee trees.

about: Pluma Hidalgo's coffee history and appellation
text: Pluma Hidalgo in Oaxaca was founded in 1880 among districts that already grew coffee, and by 1891 the Juquila district's farms had about 365,000 coffee plants. In 2020 Mexico made 'Pluma' a designation of origin for the region's coffee.

about: Black Gold film and the Oromia co-op union
text: The 2006 documentary Black Gold follows Tadesse Meskela, manager of the Oromia Coffee Farmers Co-operative Union, which then spoke for over 74,000 farmers, on his mission to keep them from going bankrupt.

about: How Best of Panama is judged
text: Best of Panama lots are cupped blind twice: first by Panamanian cuppers, then, under new code numbers, by an international jury of green-coffee buyers, while an outside auditing firm oversees the process.

about: Hacienda La Esmeralda's 2004 Gesha lot
text: Hacienda La Esmeralda in Boquete first planted Gesha for its resistance to disease. In 2004 the Petersons separated their harvest by plot for the first time, and a pure Gesha lot from their high Jaramillo farm won the Best of Panama.

about: The Philippines' 1828 coffee-planting prize
text: In 1828 the Philippines' Royal Economic Society offered a prize to whoever could plant and ripen 60,000 square feet of coffee, about 6,000 trees. Paul de La Gironière won its 1,000 pesos with his estate at Jala-Jala.

about: Barako, the Philippines' Liberica
text: In the Philippines, Liberica is known as barako. The first seedlings were planted in Amadeo, Cavite, in 1876, and its big cherries and beans come mainly from Batangas and Cavite.

about: PNG's four coffee-growing highland provinces
text: Most of Papua New Guinea's coffee is grown in a cluster of four highland provinces at the heart of the country: Western Highlands around Mount Hagen, Eastern Highlands around Goroka and Kainantu, and Jiwaka and Chimbu between them.

about: PNG's coffee grades, from A and B to Y
text: Papua New Guinea's grades long showed who grew the coffee: estate lots from mills near the highlands' only highway carried grades such as A and B, while bulked village coffee went all the way down to grade Y.

about: PNG's plantation partnerships, 1950s-70s
text: From the 1950s to the 1970s, Papua New Guinea's coffee grew through partnerships: European plantation owners taught highland farmers to grow and pick ripe cherries, and set up mills and buyer networks for them. That support faded around independence in 1975.

about: Papua New Guinea's smallholder gardens
text: More than 85 percent of Papua New Guinea's coffee comes from village smallholders, who grow it in gardens of up to two hectares. Coffee is a key source of income for more than 2.5 million people there.

about: Puerto Rico, sixth-largest producer in 1896
text: Puerto Rico was a coffee heavyweight in the 1800s: in 1896 the island ranked sixth among all the world's coffee producers.

about: Quindío's committee and the Parque del Café
text: Quindío's coffee growers' committee was founded in 1966, the same year as the department itself. The opening of the Parque del Café in 1995 was a turning point for the region's tourism.

about: Santander's shade-grown coffee
text: Santander's coffee zone is known above all for growing coffee under shade, which keeps temperatures even so the cherries ripen slowly. That shade system is part of Café de Santander's denomination of origin, granted in 2014.

about: Indigenous coffee in the Sierra Nevada
text: In the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, indigenous communities took up coffee in the late 20th century. It has since become the area's main crop, grown in the shade of native and fruit trees, much of it organically.

about: Mandheling as a broad Sumatran trade name
text: On a bag, 'Mandheling' is more a trade name than a place: it is often used for any wet-hulled coffee from Sumatra, even coffee grown in Aceh.

about: Alishan's tea pickers turned coffee pickers
text: Alishan, in Taiwan's Chiayi County, made its name with tea as well as coffee, and many of its coffee pickers used to pick tea; one local expert says they found coffee the easier job. Its farms lie at about 1,000 to 1,400 m.

about: Taiwan's 'Typica' that turned out to be SL34
text: The Japanese first planted Typica in Taiwan, and most of the island's coffee trees were assumed to be Typica. Genetic tests, one local expert says, showed that many are in fact SL34, a variety that looks very similar.

about: CoopeTarrazú's founding in 1960
text: Tarrazú's big co-op, CoopeTarrazú, was founded on 13 October 1960 by 228 small growers. Its first mill was an old one with outdated machinery, where it took in its first 6,000 fanegas of coffee; in the 2018–19 harvest it received 272,000.

about: Doi Chaang's Akha growers and their own brand
text: In Doi Chaang village in Chiang Rai, mostly Akha growers, helped by a Canadian businessman, did something unusual for smallholders: they sold nearly all their coffee roasted, under the Doi Chaang name, in Thailand, elsewhere in Asia and in Canada.

about: Thailand's Royal Project and arabica
text: Thailand's Royal Project, set up by King Bhumibol after a 1969 visit to Chiang Mai province, has worked with other agencies to bring more than 150 new crops to highland farmers who grew opium poppies. Arabica coffee is one of them.

about: Timor-Leste's de facto organic coffee
text: Most of Timor-Leste's coffee trees are arabica-robusta crosses, tended by smallholders. Decades of neglect left many groves free of farm chemicals, so its coffee has often been certified organic.

about: Tolima's two flowerings a year
text: Tolima's warm climate lets its coffee trees flower twice a year, one of the traits behind Café del Tolima's denomination of origin, protected since 2017.

about: Key Coffee's 1970s Toraja revival
text: Toraja's coffee farms were abandoned in the Second World War. When an executive of Japan's Kimura Coffee, now Key Coffee, reached the highlands in 1973, he found farmers still growing a little, and in 1978 it returned to market as Toarco Toraja.

about: Where the Toraja and Kalossi names come from
text: Toraja coffee is named after the Toraja people of Sulawesi's highlands, and Tana Toraja means 'Torajaland'. In Dutch colonial days the same coffee went by Kalossi, the name of a regional market town.

about: Venezuela's coffee overtakes cacao, 1809
text: In 1809 Venezuela exported more than 7 million pounds of coffee, enough to draw level with cacao, which then fell further and further behind.

about: Coffee's arrival in Venezuela's Orinoco, 1730
text: Coffee reached Venezuela in 1730 with the religious missions of the Orinoco region. In 1741 José Gumilla wrote that he had planted it himself and found the land well suited to plentiful harvests.

about: Café Veracruz appellation of origin, 2000
text: In 2000 Mexico protected 'Café Veracruz' as a designation of origin covering the whole state. The declaration credits deep volcanic soils, a humid, cloudy climate and a long local habit of fermenting coffee straight after pulping.

about: Vietnam's 1986 bet on coffee
text: In 1986 Vietnam's government chose coffee as one of a few crops to invest in, and production grew steadily through the late 1980s and 1990s. About 95 percent of Vietnam's coffee is robusta.

about: Why Vietnamese coffee uses condensed milk
text: Vietnam's condensed-milk coffee dates from coffee's arrival in the 19th century, when fresh milk was hard to find and condensed milk kept without refrigeration.

about: Vietnam's phin filter and dark roast
text: Traditional Vietnamese coffee is usually roasted dark and made in a phin filter, and some of it is mixed with chicory or corn.

about: Café Villa Rica's denomination of origin
text: In 2010 Peru's intellectual property office, Indecopi, made Café Villa Rica a denomination of origin. It covers coffee from the Villa Rica district of Oxapampa province, in Pasco, central Peru.

about: Villa Sarchí, a Bourbon mutant from the West Valley
text: Villa Sarchí, a compact mutant of Bourbon that arose naturally, was first singled out in Costa Rica's West Valley. It is sometimes sold on its own, unmixed with other varieties.

about: Yayu's wild coffee forest reserve
text: Yayu, in Ethiopia's Illubabor zone, keeps one of the last patches of montane rainforest where Arabica still grows wild. Since 2010 it has been a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and its core and buffer zones are officially recognised as a place to conserve forest coffee.

about: Father Liétard's coffee trees in Zhukula
text: Coffee came to Yunnan with a French missionary, Father Alfred Liétard, who grew it beside his church. In 2022, 24 coffee trees more than a century old still stood in Zhukula, a village outside Dali.

about: Yunnan's share of China's coffee
text: About 98 percent of China's coffee is grown in Yunnan, in the south-west, with Hainan and Fujian provinces growing the rest.

about: Nestlé, Yunnan and Catimor in 1988
text: In 1988 Nestlé joined Yunnan's government in planting Catimor across the province, a rust-resistant variety that a government programme had brought in from Portugal in the 1980s.

about: Anaerobic: a ferment, not a whole process
text: 'Anaerobic' on a bag describes the fermentation, not the whole process: a ferment sealed off from oxygen can lead into a natural, a honey or a washed coffee.

about: Anaerobic barrels and the one-way valve
text: In anaerobic processing, coffee ferments in sealed barrels topped with a one-way valve: the gases fermentation gives off push the oxygen out, and no fresh air can get back in.

about: Best of Panama's 2024 additive ban
text: In 2024 the Best of Panama competition barred coffees found to have been altered with foreign additives, saying it wanted to safeguard the identity of Panama's coffee. The decision drew mixed reactions.

about: Carbonic maceration's winemaking roots
text: Carbonic maceration borrows its name from winemaking, where whole bunches of grapes ferment in tanks. In coffee, whole cherries are shut in airtight tanks and flooded with carbon dioxide, which drives the oxygen out.

about: Saša Šestić's 2015 carbonic maceration win
text: Saša Šestić of Australia won the 2015 World Barista Championship in Seattle with a routine that included a cappuccino made from half natural and half washed carbonic maceration coffee.

about: Co-ferments vs yeast-inoculated coffees
text: What makes a co-ferment different from a yeast-inoculated coffee? As Diego Robelo of Costa Rica's Aquiares Estate puts it, a co-ferment adds not only new microbes but a new sugar source, such as fresh fruit pulp.

about: Kurt Zosel's chance CO2 decaf find
text: CO2 decaf was found by accident: in 1967 Kurt Zosel of Germany's Max Planck Institute for Coal Research, studying new ways to separate mixtures, noticed that caffeine dissolves in supercritical carbon dioxide.

about: Costa Rica's eco-pulpers
text: An eco-pulper rubs the sticky fruit flesh off the beans by machine instead of fermenting it away. Mario Arroyo of ICAFE, Costa Rica's coffee institute, describes it as mechanical demucilaging that cuts water use.

about: Costa Rica's micro-mill revolution
text: Costa Rican farmers used to deliver their cherries to large central mills, where coffee was bulked by region. Farms with their own small mills changed that, a shift exporter Francisco Mena dubbed the 'micromill revolution'.

about: Ethiopia's late start with washed coffee
text: Until the 1970s, all of Ethiopia's coffee was natural, dried in the fruit. Washing came to southern Ethiopia only then, though Yirgacheffe and Sidamo went on to be best known for washed coffees.

about: Pulped natural in Brazil, honey in Costa Rica
text: Brazil pioneered drying pulped coffee with its fruit layer still on, and still calls it 'pulped natural'. Costa Rica popularised the name honey, and the idea of using the method for small, carefully made lots.

about: How mills make yellow, red and black honeys
text: Honey colours have no single recipe. Many mills set yellow, red or black by how much mucilage a machine strips off; Costa Rica's Las Lajas leaves it all on and steers the colour by how it dries the coffee.

about: Las Lajas and the 2008 earthquake
text: When a 2008 earthquake left Costa Rica's Las Lajas mill without water for weeks in the middle of harvest, Oscar Chacón looked to dry-process countries such as Brazil and Ethiopia for ideas, and switched to honeys.

about: Why the honey process is called honey
text: No honey goes into honey-process coffee. The name comes from the sticky mucilage left on the beans while they dry, which people likened to honey.

about: Infused, flavoured or co-fermented
text: Infused coffees, which can have extracts or essential oils added, appeared in the late 2010s alongside co-ferments. The words 'infused', 'flavoured' and 'co-fermented' are often used as if they meant the same thing.

about: Kenya's washing channels and paddles
text: Kenyan factories finish washing in concrete channels, where workers push the parchment against running water with wooden paddles. The same step sorts the coffee by weight into grades.

about: Why Kenya began double washing
text: Kenya's 'double washing' began as a way to wait for space: when the drying beds were full, washed parchment was held underwater, where it stayed cool and out of insects' reach, until there was room to dry it.

about: Where Kenya's sorted-out cherries go
text: At Kenyan factories, cherries sorted out before pulping go to the dry method: they are dried whole, then hulled, losing their dried pulp and parchment in a single step.

about: Kenya's named drying stages
text: In Kenya, drying parchment passes through named stages: skin drying, then the white stage, soft black and hard black, as its moisture falls from about 55% to about 12%.

about: The gritty test for Kenyan fermentation
text: At Kenyan coffee factories, fermenting off the mucilage takes one to four days, faster in warm weather. Workers know it is done when a rinsed sample of parchment feels gritty.

about: Lactic bacteria before the fermentation tank
text: Microbes get going before the fermentation tank: on an experimental farm in Ecuador, researchers found lactic acid bacteria already thriving while the picked cherries were gathered and waited to be pulped.

about: Longer ferments and Lactobacillus in Ecuador
text: In an Ecuadorian trial, stretching a washed fermentation from 16 to 64 hours shifted the tank from Leuconostoc to Lactobacillus bacteria, and the green beans ended up with five times as much lactic acid.

about: How Monsooned Malabar is made
text: Monsooned Malabar is made from June to September in open-sided warehouses on India's south-west coast. Over 12 to 16 weeks in the damp monsoon air, the beans swell to nearly twice their size and turn straw yellow.

about: Monsooning's sailing-ship origin story
text: India's Coffee Board traces monsooning to the days of sail, when coffee shipped to Europe met the monsoon winds and arrived swollen and changed in colour. Today the beans are monsooned on land, on purpose.

about: Natural process: little water, dry climates
text: Drying coffee in its fruit takes little water or electricity, unlike running a wet mill, but it only suits places with reliably dry weather.

about: How long natural coffee dries
text: A natural coffee dries whole, cherry and all, for two to six weeks in the sun, spread in thin layers and turned regularly to slow fermentation and keep mould and rot away.

about: Reposo: resting coffee in parchment
text: Once dried, coffee often rests in its parchment for about six to eight weeks before export, a stage called reposo. In a study of Bolivian lots, rested coffee kept a slightly steadier water activity, reacting less to swings in humidity and temperature.

about: Ludwig Roselius and Kaffee HAG
text: Decaf began in Bremen: coffee merchant Ludwig Roselius patented a method using benzene as the solvent in 1905, and founded Kaffee HAG the following year.

about: How sugarcane (EA) decaf is made
text: For 'sugarcane' decaf, green beans are steamed for half an hour, then bathed in water and ethyl acetate made by fermenting sugarcane, the tank drained and refilled over about eight hours. A last steaming drives off the solvent.

about: Swiss Water decaf: hot water and charcoal
text: The Swiss Water Process, made commercially viable by the Swiss firm Coffex in the 1980s, uses no solvents: hot water draws the caffeine out of green beans and activated charcoal catches it.

about: Thermal shock: hot and cold rinses
text: In thermal shock processing, fermented beans get hot and then cold rinses. For one Colombian lot from Wilton Benitez, the aim was to help the beans take up what fermentation produced and to stop the fermentation.

about: Low oxygen in underwater fermentation
text: Even a classic washed fermentation runs low on oxygen once the coffee is under water. Researchers found that a longer ferment strengthened the effect of that hypoxia on the beans' own metabolism.

about: Water activity vs moisture in green coffee
text: Moisture content counts all the water in a green bean; water activity gauges how much of it is free to take part in reactions, on a scale where pure water is 1.0. One long-term study put the best range for green coffee at about 0.45 to 0.55.

about: Why water activity matters in storage
text: Water activity matters in stored green coffee: with too much free water, moulds and fungi can grow; with too little, the living seed lacks the water its enzymes need.

about: The blue-green look of wet-hulled beans
text: Wet-hulled green coffee is easy to spot: the beans come out a dark, mottled green, and some people describe them as blue.

about: Why wet-hulled coffee dries faster
text: In Indonesia's humid climate, hulling early pays off: with the parchment gone, the sun reaches the bean directly and it dries two to three times faster.

about: Kuku kambing, the 'goat's nail' split
text: Hulling beans that are still soft and full of water takes care, as the machines can split them at the ends. In Indonesia a bean split this way is called kuku kambing, 'goat's nail', after its shape.

about: Wet-hulling: parchment off mid-drying
text: Wet-hulled coffee is stripped of its parchment halfway through drying, while the beans still hold about 20 to 40% moisture. They finish drying bare, down to about 12 to 13%.

about: Yeast inoculation, borrowed from brewing
text: Yeast-inoculated coffees borrow a trick from brewing and winemaking: producers add chosen strains of yeast to the coffee before or during fermentation.

about: Yemen's millstone hulling, camels to engines
text: In Yemen, dried coffee cherries have long been husked between millstones. The stones were once turned by camels; engines do the job now.

about: Colin Harmon's four Irish barista titles
text: Colin Harmon of Dublin's 3fe won the Irish Barista Championship four times.

about: How 3fe (Third Floor Espresso) got its name
text: 3fe is short for Third Floor Espresso: founder Colin Harmon trained for the 2009 World Barista Championship in a room of his third-floor flat, and his designers suggested naming the shop after it.

about: Black & White's start with Back Alley Coffee
text: Lem Butler won the US Barista Championship in 2016 and Kyle Ramage in 2017; after Ramage's win the pair bought Back Alley Coffee Roasters in Wake Forest, North Carolina, as the start of Black & White.

about: Black & White's two barista-champion founders
text: Black & White Coffee Roasters was founded in 2017 by Kyle Ramage and Lem Butler, two US Barista Champions who wanted more people to drink the kind of coffee they had met in competition.

about: Blue Bottle's clarinettist founder and potting shed
text: Blue Bottle's founder James Freeman spent about ten years as a working clarinettist around the Bay Area before turning to coffee; the company began in a tiny former potting shed beside his Oakland flat, where he roasted the beans.

about: Blue Bottle's first bag at Old Oakland market
text: Blue Bottle's founder James Freeman sold his first bag of coffee at the Old Oakland Farmers Market, which was the first in the Bay Area to let his new roasting business take a stall.

about: Coffee Collective's first days on Jægersborggade
text: Coffee Collective first served coffee to the public at a farmers' market on Copenhagen's Jægersborggade in August 2007, while roasting near Kastrup Airport; its first shop opened on the same street in February 2008.

about: Coffee Collective's founding and Klaus Thomsen
text: Copenhagen's Coffee Collective was founded in 2007, and one of its founders, Klaus Thomsen, is a former World Barista Champion.

about: Counter Culture's first bag, sold in Durham
text: Counter Culture Coffee sold its very first bag in 1995 to Pop's Trattoria, a restaurant in Durham, North Carolina, just three months after Brett Smith and Fred Houk came up with the idea for the company.

about: Counter Culture's 2013 tasters' flavour wheel
text: In 2013 Counter Culture's coffee-buying team drew up its own tasters' flavour wheel as a learning aid for anyone who tastes coffee; for a word on it that is new to a taster, a reference can probably be found at a local supermarket.

about: Joanna Alm's roasting titles
text: Drop Coffee's Joanna Alm is a three-time Swedish Coffee Roasting Champion and has more than once finished in the top three at the World Coffee Roasting Championship.

about: Drop Coffee's start near Mariatorget
text: Drop Coffee opened in 2009 as a coffee bar near Mariatorget in Stockholm; a year later it started roasting on a 1 kg roaster at the back of the shop, and moved up to a 25 kg Diedrich in 2012.

about: How Rubens Gardelli started roasting
text: Rubens Gardelli caught the roasting bug after spotting a roaster on show in a bar in California; back in Italy in October 2008, he began experimenting with a small copper roaster on his home stove.

about: Rubens Gardelli's roasting titles
text: Rubens Gardelli of Forlì won the Italian Roasting Championship every year from 2014 to 2017, and in 2014 he also came second in the world at the Brewers Cup.

about: George Howell and the Cup of Excellence
text: George Howell co-founded the Cup of Excellence in 1999, setting up the first international competition and online auction for coffees from single estates.

about: George Howell Coffee and Extract MoJo
text: George Howell Coffee helped finance and introduce Extract MoJo, which it calls the first refractometer-and-software system made for coffee.

about: Intelligentsia's first café in Lakeview, Chicago
text: On 9 October 1995 Doug Zell and Emily Mange opened Intelligentsia, a café and roastery in Chicago's Lakeview neighbourhood, where they roasted the beans in the shop on a Probat L12.

about: Michael Phillips, first American world barista champion
text: In June 2010 Intelligentsia barista Michael Phillips won the World Barista Championship in London, ahead of competitors from 52 other countries, and became the first American to take the title.

about: Koppi's founders in Helsingborg
text: Koppi was founded in Helsingborg, Sweden, in 2007 by Anne Lunell and Charles Nystrand, a pair of barista and brewing competition champions.

about: Koppi's move from coffee bar to roastery
text: Koppi began as a coffee bar in the heart of Helsingborg with its roaster right in the shop; in 2016 it moved into an old industrial building to concentrate on roasting alone.

about: La Cabra's start in Aarhus
text: La Cabra was set up in Aarhus, Denmark, in 2011 and began sourcing and roasting its own coffee two years later, in 2013.

about: La Cabra's one roast profile per coffee
text: La Cabra settles on one roast profile for each coffee at the cupping table, rather than roasting it one way for filter and another for espresso.

about: Market Lane's founding in Melbourne
text: Fleur Studd and Jason Scheltus founded Market Lane in Melbourne in 2009, when, as they tell it, coffee that was fresh, seasonal and traceable was nearly impossible to find in Australia.

about: Market Lane's first shop in Prahran Market
text: Market Lane opened its first shop and roastery inside Melbourne's Prahran Market, among shoppers who hunt for good produce and care about where and when it was grown.

about: ONA Coffee's garage start in Canberra
text: ONA Coffee began in 2008, when Saša Šestić, a former Olympic handball player, started roasting coffee in his garage in Canberra.

about: ONA's world titles: Šestić and Chu
text: ONA's founder Saša Šestić won the World Barista Championship in 2015, and ONA's Charlie Chu became World Cup Tasters Champion in 2021.

about: Onyx at the 2020 US coffee championships
text: At the 2020 US coffee championships in California, Onyx Coffee Lab's Andrea Allen won the US Barista Championship, while her Onyx colleagues Elika Liftee and Lance Hedrick came first and second in the Brewers Cup.

about: Onyx Coffee Lab's start in Springdale
text: Jon and Andrea Allen started Onyx Coffee Lab in May 2012 as a small café in Springdale, Arkansas, with a staff of ten.

about: How Major Dickason's Blend got its name
text: Peet's Major Dickason's Blend is named after Key Dickason, a retired army sergeant and friend of Alfred Peet who suggested the idea in 1969; the finished blend was thought good enough to promote him to major.

about: Peet's first shop at Vine and Walnut, 1966
text: Alfred Peet, who learned the trade looking after the roasting machinery at his father's small coffee firm in the Netherlands, opened his own coffee shop on 1 April 1966 at the corner of Vine and Walnut streets in Berkeley, California.

about: How Phil and Sebastian met
text: Sebastian Sztabzyb and his business partner Phil met in 1996, paired as lab partners in a digital circuits class while both studied engineering at the University of Calgary, years before they opened Phil & Sebastian in 2007.

about: Phil & Sebastian's rebuilt Probat UG-15
text: Phil & Sebastian's first production roaster was a 55-year-old Probat UG-15, rebuilt by Giesen in the Netherlands; it arrived coated in surface rust, and after 15 hours of scrubbing the first test roasts ran in June 2009.

about: Pilot Coffee Roasters' garage start
text: Pilot Coffee Roasters began in May 2009, when Andy Wilkin, newly qualified as a Q Grader, and Jessie Holmes opened a café and micro-roastery in a former car garage in Toronto's Leslieville.

about: Pilot's first name, Te Aro Roasted
text: Pilot started life as Te Aro Roasted, a café inspired by the ones Andy Wilkin had admired in his home town, Te Aro in Wellington, New Zealand; by 2013 it had become Pilot Coffee Roasters.

about: Square Mile's founders and founding year
text: Square Mile Coffee Roasters was founded in London in 2008 by Anette Moldvaer and James Hoffmann.

about: James Hoffmann's 2007 world title in Tokyo
text: Square Mile co-founder James Hoffmann won the World Barista Championship in Tokyo in 2007, competing as the UK's barista champion.

about: Stumptown's one-person start in 1999
text: Stumptown began in Portland in 1999 with a staff of one, a small vintage Probat roaster and a Ford Pinto to deliver the beans.

about: Stumptown's Hair Bender café and blend
text: Stumptown's first café opened on Portland's Division Street in 1999 in what had been a beauty parlour called Hair Bender, and founder Duane Sorenson kept the name for the house espresso blend.

about: Tim Wendelboe's competition record
text: Tim Wendelboe came second at the World Barista Championship in 2001 and 2002 and won it in 2004, a run that later helped him open his own café and roastery in Oslo's Grünerløkka. He was also World Cup Tasters Champion in 2005.

about: Tim Wendelboe's farm, Finca El Suelo
text: Tim Wendelboe owns and runs Finca El Suelo, a 7-hectare farm at about 1,650–1,700 m in El Pital, Huila, Colombia, which he treats as a learning project in regenerative farming; its first cherries were picked in 2021.

about: Agtron numbers, whole bean and ground
text: On the Agtron scale, a higher number means a lighter roast. Coffee Review reads each coffee both as whole beans and ground: the lightest roasts score about 70 as beans but about 95 once ground.

about: Jabez Burns and the corn popper
text: Jabez Burns invented the continuous roaster, forerunner of today's production machines, yet he claimed a simple corn popper had roasted some of the best coffee he ever drank.

about: Chaff, the silverskin shed in the roast
text: The papery flakes a roaster blows out are chaff: the silverskin, the thin outer layer of the coffee bean, which loosens and comes away in the heat of the roast.

about: Cooling a roast in under four minutes
text: Beans keep roasting on their own heat once they leave the drum, so roasters aim to cool them to room temperature in under about four minutes. Most drum roasters use a perforated tray, a stirring arm and a fan drawing room air through.

about: The sound of first and second crack
text: A University of Texas acoustics study recorded beans as they roasted: first crack was louder and lower-pitched than second crack, whose pops came thick and fast. The aim was to see whether a machine could follow a roast by ear.

about: Why very dark roasts look oily
text: Pressure inside a roasting bean pushes its oils from the middle of each cell towards the surface. In very dark roasts that oil can make it all the way out, where you can see it on the beans.

about: Roasted beans: less dense, more porous
text: A roasting bean swells even as it loses weight, so its density falls the whole way through. The roast also opens up pores inside it, leaving the bean far more soluble than it was when green.

about: Development time ratio
text: Development time ratio is the share of a roast that comes after first crack. End a ten-and-a-half-minute roast 40 seconds into first crack, and the ratio is about 6%.

about: A falling rate of rise
text: Many roasters aim for a rate of rise that falls steadily through a roast: the beans keep getting hotter, but each minute adds a little less, so the curve gently flattens.

about: First crack at about 193 °C
text: First crack comes at a bean temperature of roughly 193 °C, as moisture inside the bean turns to steam and its cells swell.

about: Maillard and caramelisation temperatures
text: In the roaster, Maillard reactions between carbohydrates and amino acids get going at about 150 °C, and caramelisation follows from about 170 °C.

about: Why roasting turns beans brown
text: Unroasted coffee is really blue-green. It turns brown in the roaster thanks to melanoidins, large molecules built when sugars and amino acids join together under heat.

about: Water in green and roasted beans
text: Green coffee is about 10 to 12% water, and a roast brings that down to around 2.5%. Not all the steam was there at the start: the roast's own chemical reactions make extra water along the way.

about: Probat's 1868 start in Emmerich
text: Probat began in 1868 in Emmerich, Germany, as a machine works and iron foundry, and built its Emmerich Spherical Roaster in 1870. The company only took the name Probat in 1959.

about: Quakers, pale beans from unripe cherries
text: Quakers are beans from unripe cherries. They are hard to spot while green, but roast to a paler brown than the rest of the batch, because they have fewer of the sugars the Maillard reaction needs.

about: Roast names follow no standard
text: Roast names like French, Italian or Viennese follow no agreed standard, so one roaster's Viennese can be quite unlike another's, as Coffee Review points out.

about: Sample roasting before buying green coffee
text: Before buying green coffee, roasters sample-roast small lots, typically 50 to 200 g, often on multi-barrel drum roasters that handle several samples at once, then cup them within 8 to 24 hours.

about: What causes second crack
text: Second crack is driven by gases, mostly carbon dioxide, building up inside the bean until its structure gives way. There is no third crack: after the second, beans simply keep darkening.

about: Michael Sivetz and fluid-bed roasters
text: Hot-air, or fluid-bed, roasters trace back to a 1970s design by engineer Michael Sivetz. In place of a drum, a strong blower keeps the beans moving through hot air, so almost no heat reaches them by contact.

about: The turning point on a roast graph
text: On a roast graph, bean temperature dips at the start before it climbs. The beans are warming all along: the cool batch is simply drawing heat from the drum and the probe. The low point is called the turning point.

about: Water quenching at the end of a roast
text: Some roasteries stop a roast with a spray of water as well as air, which is called quenching. It is mostly kept for commercial-grade coffee rather than specialty lots.

about: Weight lost in the roast
text: Beans leave the roaster about 12 to 20% lighter, from lost water and from solid matter turned into gas. Many roasters track that loss, and an odd number flags a batch for a closer look.

about: Lockhart's 1957 brewing control chart
text: The brewing chart baristas still train with dates from 1957, when Lockhart tied coffee quality to two numbers: strength, the share of the drink that is dissolved coffee, and extraction, the share of the grounds dissolved. Its 'ideal' box: 1.15–1.35% and 18–22%.

about: Why yields fall at the finest grinds
text: A 2020 model of espresso predicted that grinding finer should always extract more, but experiments found yields falling at the finest settings, a sign that water was no longer flowing evenly through the puck.

about: Grinding cold beans for a narrower spread
text: Cold beans shatter more evenly: a 2016 study ground coffee at 20 °C, −19 °C, −79 °C and −196 °C (room, freezer, dry ice and liquid nitrogen), and grinding cold gave a narrower spread of particle sizes and a smaller average.

about: Bicarbonate in water as a source of crema gas
text: Not all of crema's gas comes from the beans: bicarbonate in the brewing water also gives off CO2, both as it breaks down in the heat and as coffee's own acids neutralise it.

about: Why crema's bubbles stay tiny
text: Crema's bubbles stay tiny partly because they have so little room: in a standard espresso cup they rise only about 1.5 to 2 cm, and specks of coffee and cell-wall fragments in the drink may act as seeds for them.

about: How dissolved CO2 may make crema
text: A 2011 review suggests crema starts in the puck: hot water under pressure dissolves the coffee's CO2, and by the authors' estimate the shot then holds about twice the gas it can keep at normal pressure, so it fizzes into tiny bubbles.

about: Why crema fades
text: One suggested reason crema thins: the hot drink evaporates water from the films between its bubbles until they break. A review of espresso foam says it should still last at least a couple of minutes before a dark spot shows.

about: Espresso as a fast transfer of CO2
text: A 2011 review of espresso foam likened espresso brewing to a fast transfer of CO2 from ground coffee into a cup. The gas comes from roasting: CO2 makes up about 87% of the gases roasted coffee gives off.

about: Coffee particles coating crema bubbles
text: Under a microscope, a bubble in freshly made espresso foam can be seen coated with coffee particles smaller than 50 microns, which researchers think may help hold crema together.

about: Weighing the gas that roasted coffee gives off
text: Roasting fills coffee's porous beans with gas, much of it CO2. Some escapes in the roaster; the rest seeps out slowly in storage and in a rush at grinding. Swiss researchers tracked it by weighing coffee on a precision balance as the gas left.

about: Distilled water in espresso machines
text: Distilled water is a poor choice for an espresso machine: very pure water is corrosive under heat and pressure, and La Marzocco notes its machines may not even recognise it, flashing the water light with a full tank.

about: Why fines extract fastest
text: In ground coffee the tiniest particles provide most of the surface water can reach, so they extract faster than the bigger pieces, a 2016 grinding study notes; a few very large particles still matter too.

about: How much CO2 grinding releases
text: Grinding breaks open the cells that hold roasted coffee's CO2: one study found more than 70% of the gas escaped when beans were ground to 500-micron particles, which is why espresso is brewed soon after grinding.

about: Headspace and extraction on a Decent DE1
text: Headspace matters: when the gap above the puck was reduced on a Decent DE1, a dark-roast 1:1 ristretto averaged an extraction yield 3.4% higher over ten shots, probably because the puck prewetted more evenly.

about: Why espresso is brewed at 9 bar
text: Why 9 bar? Decent's blog traces it to the springs of Achille Gaggia's late-1940s lever machines, which happened to give about 8 to 10 bar, and finds no documented testing behind the number.

about: Puck screens and water at the basket's edges
text: Puck screens, coarse metal meshes laid on the coffee, add little resistance but can reshape how water spreads. With a traditional basket, one test found extraction about 1.8% higher, likely because the mesh sends water toward the edges.

about: How the Ross droplet technique changed espresso
text: Wetting the beans changed the espresso too: in a 2023 study, dark roasts ground with a few drops of water ran slower and gave shots at least 15% more concentrated.

about: The Ross droplet technique and static
text: The 'Ross droplet technique' means wetting beans with a few drops of water before grinding. In a 2023 study, 20 to 30 microlitres per gram cut the static charge on the grounds by at least half.

about: How a coffee refractometer works
text: A coffee refractometer reads strength from how much a sample bends light, measuring its temperature at the same time; VST, the company of Vince Fedele, made the first one designed specifically for coffee.

about: SCA home-brewer temperature rule
text: When a 2020 study was written, SCA home-brewer certification required a drip coffee maker to reach 92 °C within the first minute of brewing, hold at least that for the rest of the cycle and never exceed 96 °C.

about: Static on ground coffee, like volcanic ash
text: Freshly ground coffee can carry static charge on the scale of volcanic ash and thundercloud ice, a 2023 study found, and some dark roasts even let off millimetre-long sparks.

about: La Marzocco's water specification
text: La Marzocco asks for water with 90 to 150 ppm of dissolved solids, 70 to 100 ppm total hardness and 40 to 80 ppm alkalinity; much more mineral-rich water tends to coat the machine in limescale.

about: WDT and John Weiss
text: WDT is the Weiss Distribution Technique, after John Weiss, who holds a biochemistry doctorate and taught computer science; he shared it online in December 2005, stirring the grounds with a dissecting needle inside a cut-down yoghurt cup.

about: Arabica, a natural hybrid of two species
text: Arabica is itself a natural hybrid: its parents were two other coffee species, Coffea canephora (robusta) and Coffea eugenioides. A 2024 genome study dates the event that founded it to roughly 350,000 to 610,000 years ago.

about: Batian, Kenya's 2010 variety
text: Batian, released in Kenya in 2010, was bred at the Ruiru coffee research station from a mix of parents including SL28, SL34, Rume Sudan and the Timor Hybrid, to stand up to both coffee leaf rust and coffee berry disease.

about: Bourbon in Brazil and its descendants
text: The Bourbon variety reached Brazil around 1860 and spread north through South and Central America, where its own descendants, Caturra, Catuaí and Mundo Novo among them, have since taken over most of its ground.

about: Bourbon's name and Réunion island
text: Red and yellow Bourbon owe their name to an island: French missionaries took the Bourbon variety from Yemen to Bourbon Island, now La Réunion, in the early 1700s, and it did not leave the island until the mid-19th century.

about: Catimor: a group, not one variety
text: Catimor is often taken for a single variety, but it is a whole group of distinct varieties sharing the same kind of parentage: Caturra crossed with the Timor Hybrid. The original crosses were made at CIFC, Portugal's coffee rust research centre.

about: Catuaí: a 1949 cross named 'very good'
text: Catuaí was bred in Brazil in 1949 by crossing yellow Caturra with Mundo Novo. Its name comes from a Guarani phrase meaning 'very good', and it comes in both yellow- and red-fruited forms.

about: Caturra's spread and close planting
text: Caturra was never officially released in Brazil, where it was found, yet it became common across Central America. Breeders were drawn to its small size, which lets the trees be planted closer together.

about: Colombia's renewal from Caturra to Castillo
text: Caturra was once thought to make up nearly half of Colombia's coffee, until a government programme from 2008 encouraged farmers to replace more than three billion trees with Castillo, a rust-resistant variety with Caturra in its parentage.

about: Caturra: the Guarani word for small
text: Caturra takes its name from a Guarani word meaning 'small'. Found on a farm in Minas Gerais, Brazil, between 1915 and 1918, it is a natural mutant of Bourbon whose single altered gene keeps the plant compact.

about: Centroamericano, a 2010 F1 hybrid
text: Centroamericano, an F1 hybrid of T5296 and Rume Sudan, was released for Central American farmers in 2010. In breeding trials it out-yielded the region's standard varieties by 22 to 47%, and it was bred to resist coffee leaf rust.

about: Ethiopia's berry-disease-resistant varieties
text: Since the 1970s, Ethiopia has released coffee varieties developed to resist coffee berry disease, and many were planted in and around its wild coffee forests, which scientists warn could let them interbreed with, and replace, the original wild gene pool.

about: 'Heirloom' and 'landrace' on Ethiopian bags
text: 'Heirloom' on an Ethiopian coffee is a loose label for arabica whose exact variety is hard to pin down: Ethiopia has thousands of coffee varieties. Several roasters now call them 'landrace' instead.

about: Excelsa and the proposed liberica split
text: Excelsa has generally been classed as a variety of liberica, Coffea liberica var. dewevrei, but a 2025 genomic study proposes splitting liberica into three species: Coffea liberica, Coffea dewevrei (excelsa) and Coffea klainei.

about: Gesha's Best of Panama breakthrough
text: Gesha's big break came when the Peterson family of Boquete, Panama, entered it in the Best of Panama competition and auction: it scored remarkably well and fetched what was then a record price for green coffee at auction.

about: Gesha's brittle branches in 1960s Panama
text: Gesha was handed out across Panama in the 1960s for its tolerance of leaf rust, yet few farmers planted it: they disliked its brittle branches.

about: Gesha's route from Ethiopia to CATIE
text: Gesha took the long road: collected from Ethiopian coffee forests in the 1930s, it went to Tanzania's Lyamungu research station, then in 1953 to the CATIE research centre in Central America, where it was logged as accession T2722.

about: Gesha grown widely in Malawi
text: Gesha is not only a Panamanian story: World Coffee Research notes that the variety is also grown widely in Malawi.

about: Gesha or Geisha: the spelling
text: Gesha or Geisha? Early gene-bank records wrote 'Geisha', but the Ethiopian forest where it was collected lies near a mountain usually written 'Gesha' in English, so many in coffee now prefer that spelling.

about: The Java variety's Ethiopian roots
text: Despite its name, the Java variety is an Ethiopian landrace selection: the Dutch took it from Ethiopia straight to the island of Java in the early 19th century. Panama, in 2016, was the first Central American country to recognise it officially.

about: Bourbon Pointu (Laurina), the pointed bean
text: Bourbon Pointu, botanically Laurina, is a natural mutation of Bourbon first selected on Réunion. 'Pointu' means pointed, after its small beans that taper at the ends, and the variety is known for being naturally low in caffeine.

about: Maragogipe, the big-bean Typica mutant
