text: Maragogipe, a natural Typica mutant found near the Brazilian city of that name in 1870, does everything big: its beans, its leaves and the lengths of stem between them are all especially large.

about: Mundo Novo, found in São Paulo in 1943
text: Mundo Novo is a natural cross of Bourbon and Typica that turned up in 1943 in São Paulo state, Brazil. It has been handed out to Brazilian farmers since 1952.

about: Pacamara's unstable generations
text: Pacamara, a cross of Pacas and Maragogipe selected by El Salvador's coffee research institute, is a restless variety: its plants vary and do not breed true from one generation to the next.

about: Pacas and the Pacas family farm
text: Pacas, a natural mutant of Bourbon, turned up in 1949 on a farm in El Salvador's Santa Ana region owned by a family of the same name.

about: Pink Bourbon's name and its genetic tests
text: Pink Bourbon got its name from a Colombian producer whose tall, gangly trees grew among Bourbon. Genetic tests commissioned by the importer Cafe Imports in 2017 and 2023 suggest it is no Bourbon at all, but an Ethiopian landrace.

about: Why robusta must cross-pollinate
text: A robusta plant cannot pollinate its own flowers: the species must cross-pollinate, and which plants can fertilise one another is set by their genes.

about: Ruiru 11, Kenya's hand-pollinated hybrid
text: Ruiru 11, released in Kenya in 1985 and named after the coffee research station at Ruiru, is made by hand: its first-generation hybrid seed comes from breeders carrying pollen from the father lines to the mother plants.

about: Sidra's debated family tree
text: Sidra's family tree is debated. It was first reported to be a Typica and Bourbon cross from Ecuador, but some DNA tests found samples close to Ethiopian heirloom coffees, and World Coffee Research suggests the name may cover several varieties.

about: SL28 and SL34 from Scott Labs
text: The SL in SL28 and SL34 stands for Scott Laboratories, the Kenyan research labs where single trees picked out between 1935 and 1939 got the prefix SL. Forty-two trees of various origins were studied there for yield, quality, drought and disease.

about: SL28 and A.D. Trench's Tanganyika tour
text: SL28's story begins on a 1931 tour of Tanganyika, now Tanzania, by A.D. Trench of Kenya's Scott Labs. He brought back seed of a drought-resistant coffee, and in 1935 SL28 was selected from a single tree of it.

about: SL34's 'French Mission' puzzle
text: SL34 was picked from a single tree on Loresho Estate in Kabete, Kenya, labelled 'French Mission', a name usually taken to mean Bourbon. Yet genetic tests tie SL34 to the Typica group, so its origin story may be wrong.

about: Starmaya, an F1 hybrid grown from seed
text: Most F1 coffee hybrids have to be cloned or pollinated by hand, but seed producers can grow Starmaya from seed. Its mother, an Ethiopian or Sudanese landrace, is male-sterile and makes no pollen, so it is crossed with the father, Marsellesa, rather than pollinating itself.

about: Stenophylla's rediscovery in Sierra Leone
text: Coffea stenophylla, named for its narrow leaves, was once farmed across Upper West Africa, but had not been seen in the wild in Sierra Leone since 1954 until scientists rediscovered it there in 2018.

about: The Timor Hybrid and Catimor rust resistance
text: The Timor Hybrid is a natural cross of arabica and robusta that sprang up by itself on the island of Timor in the 1920s. Its robusta genes carried resistance to coffee leaf rust into the Catimor varieties bred from it.

about: Typica's decline in the Americas
text: Typica was the coffee on most South and Central American plantations until the 1940s. Its low yields and weakness against the major coffee diseases have since seen it slowly give way across much of the Americas.

about: Typica's arrival in Jamaica in 1730
text: In 1730 the English carried Typica to Jamaica from Martinique. Jamaica still plants it widely, and there it goes by the name Jamaica Blue Mountain.

about: Villa Sarchi and the Sarchimor name
text: Villa Sarchi, a dwarf Bourbon mutant, was found in Costa Rica's Alajuela province in the 1950s or 60s. It stands up to strong winds and lends half its name to the Sarchimor group of coffees.

about: Wild coffee species at risk of extinction
text: Arabica and robusta are just two of many: a 2019 assessment of all 124 wild coffee species then known found that at least 60% of them are threatened with extinction.

about: Wush Wush, named after a place
text: Like many Ethiopian heirloom coffees, Wush Wush is named after the place where it was first found: Wushwush, a small area in south-west Ethiopia. It reached South America around 1990.

about: Yellow Bourbon's debated beginnings
text: Yellow Bourbon is thought to have turned up in 1930 among the Red Bourbon on a farm near Pederneiras, in Brazil's São Paulo state. Many think it began as a natural cross of Red Bourbon with Yellow Botucatu, though some researchers suspect a mutation instead.
